arXiv:2505.02400v1 [math.PR] 05 May 2025

Spectral gap of the KMP and other stochastic
exchange models on arbitrary graphs

Seonwoo Kim Address: Yonsei University Email address: seonwookim@yonsei.ac.kr , Matteo Quattropani Address: University of Roma Tre Email address: matteo.quattropani@uniroma3.it and Federico Sau Address: University of Milan Email address: federico.sau@unimi.it
Abstract.

We present a simple strategy to derive universal bounds on the spectral gap of reversible stochastic exchange models on arbitrary graphs. The Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) model, the harmonic process (HP), and the immediate exchange model (IEM) are all examples that fall into this class. Our upper and lower bounds depend only on two features: worst-case linear statistics and a kinetic factor, which is, in essence, graph-independent. For the three aforementioned examples, these bounds are sharp, and even saturate to an identity for HP and IEM in some log-concave regimes. The proof—which yields bounds for eigenvalues even in the non-reversible context—crucially exploits the rigidity of the eigenstructure of these models and quantitative contraction rates of the corresponding hidden parameter models recently introduced in [DMFG24, GRT25].

1. Introduction. From KMP to more general exchange models

1.1. The KMP model

Consider a finite weighted undirected graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), some positive parameters α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, and the following stochastic exchange dynamics involving non-negative masses (ηx)x∈V(\eta_{x})_{x\in V} on VV. First, select a pair of vertices x,y∈Vx,y\in V with rate cx​y=cy​x≥0c_{xy}=c_{yx}\geq 0. Then, sample a random variable U∼Beta⁡(αx,αy)U\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{x},\alpha_{y}). Finally, update (ηx,ηy)(\eta_{x},\eta_{y}) to

(1.1) (U⁡(ηx+ηy),(1−U)​(ηx+ηy))​,\left(U(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y}),(1-U)(\eta_{x}+\eta_{y})\right)\;\text{,}\;\;

while leaving the other masses unchanged. This is known as the Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti (KMP) model on the graph GG with parameters α\alpha.

The original KMP model was introduced in [KMP82] to describe heat conduction along a one-dimensional segment in contact with thermal reservoirs at its endpoints. In that setting, energy is exchanged only between neighboring vertices and with the reservoirs, and the model was defined with U∼U⁡(0,1)U\sim\mathrm{U}(0,1) (i.e., αx≡1\alpha_{x}\equiv 1). This formulation has since been generalized; see, e.g., [GKRV09]. On the same segment but without reservoirs, the model has been studied more recently under the name adjacent walk on the simplex [CLL20, LP25]. More broadly, this redistribution mechanism is also known as the beta-splitting process, emphasizing the role of the UU-distribution in determining how mass is split. In the mean-field setting—where all rates cx​yc_{xy} are equal and αx≡1/2\alpha_{x}\equiv 1/2—the dynamics coincides with the evolution of particle energies in the Kac’s walk [Kac56], one of the most successful many-body mean-field models of stochastically colliding particles in kinetic theory.

In any of the above settings, the KMP model presents two key qualitative features. First, the dynamics described in (1.1) is conservative, with the transition rates not depending on the total mass. Henceforth, without loss of generality, we shall always consider only unitary masses, i.e.,

(1.2) η∈Ω≔{η=(ηx)x∈V:ηx≥0for allx∈V,|η|=1},with|η|=∑x∈Vηx.\eta\in\Omega\coloneqq\left\{\eta=(\eta_{x})_{x\in V}:\eta_{x}\geq 0\ \text{for all}\ x\in V\,,\,|\eta|=1\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{with}\ |\eta|=\sum_{x\in V}\eta_{x}\;\text{.}

Second, the KMP model on Ω\Omega admits—as soon as the underlying graph is connected—a unique, explicit, reversible measure: the Dirichlet distribution with parameters α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, written as Dir⁡(α){\rm Dir}(\alpha). Letting μ∈𝒫⁡(Ω)\mu\in\mathcal{P}(\Omega) denote this measure, this reads as

(1.3) μ⁡(d​η)=1B⁡(α)​(∏x∈Vηxαx−1)​d​η​,with​B​(α)≔1Γ⁡(|α|)​∏x∈VΓ⁡(αx)​,\mu({\rm d}\eta)=\frac{1}{{\rm B}(\alpha)}\bigg(\prod_{x\in V}\eta_{x}^{\alpha_{x}-1}\bigg){\rm d}\eta\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{with}\ {\rm B}(\alpha)\coloneqq\frac{1}{\Gamma(|\alpha|)}\prod_{x\in V}\Gamma(\alpha_{x})\;\text{,}\;\;

where d​η{\rm d}\eta stands for the uniform measure on Ω\Omega.

1.1.1. Convergence to equilibrium and spectral gap

Our primary focus is to quantify relaxation to equilibrium for this model on arbitrary graphs. Because of the aforementioned reversibility, we shall focus on the process’ spectral gap, governing the L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu)-exponential convergence rate. For more background on convergence to equilibrium, spectral gaps, and other functional inequalities for Markov processes, we refer to the monographs [BGL14, LP17].

The spectral gap of the KMP model has been completely characterized in the specific settings described above. Indeed, around two decades ago, in the mean-field setup, spectral gap estimates—and even the exact value—have been obtained in a series of influential works [Jan01, CCL03, Cap08], thereby solving Kac’s long-standing conjecture [Kac56]. More recently, [CLL20] determined the precise value of the spectral gap on the segment, whenever αx≡const.≥1\alpha_{x}\equiv{\rm const.}\geq 1; for general α\alpha, bounds were previously derived in [GKS12]. For mixing-time results, see, e.g., [RW05, CLL20, LP25] on the segment, [Smi14, CQS25] for the mean-field setup, and references therein.

All the above spectral gap results crucially exploit inherent symmetries of the underlying geometry. When moving away from such settings, establishing the precise value of the spectral gap becomes unfeasible; however, one can still resort to spectral gap comparisons, that reduce an infinite- to a finite-dimensional optimization problem. Analogous spectral-gap reductions have been observed within the context of interacting particle systems; see Section 2.3.1 below for more details.

1.1.2. KMP{\rm KMP}’s main result

By reversibility, the KMP infinitesimal generator, say ℒ\mathcal{L}, is self-adjoint in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu). In turn, the spectral gap of ℒ\mathcal{L} admits the following well-known variational formulation:

(1.4) gap⁡(G,α)=inf{𝒟⁡(f):f∈L2​(μ)​with​‖f−μ​f‖L2​(μ)=1}​,{\rm gap}(G,\alpha)=\inf\left\{\mathcal{D}(f):f\in L^{2}(\mu)\ \text{with}\ \|f-\mu f\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}=1\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

where 𝒟⁡(f)=⟨f|−ℒ​f⟩L2​(μ)\mathcal{D}(f)=\left\langle f\,\middle|\,-\mathcal{L}f\right\rangle_{L^{2}(\mu)} denotes the Dirichlet form associated to ℒ\mathcal{L}, and μ​f\mu f is a shorthand notation for ∫f​𝑑μ\int f\,{\rm d}\mu. However, thanks to the specifics of the model, the variational problem in (1.4) can be considerably simplified. Indeed, as we shall explain below (see Proposition 2.4), ℒ\mathcal{L} leaves the (finite-dimensional) space 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} of polynomials of degree kk in the variables (ηx)x∈V(\eta_{x})_{x\in V} invariant. This, combined with the aforementioned reversibility with respect to μ\mu in (1.3), ensures that gap⁡(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha) can be recovered by optimizing over each 𝒫k⊂L2​(μ)\mathscr{P}_{k}\subset L^{2}(\mu) separately:

(1.5) gap⁡(G,α)=infk≥1gapk​(G,α)​,{\rm gap}(G,\alpha)=\inf_{k\geq 1}{\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

where, for all integers k≥1k\geq 1,

(1.6) gapk​(G,α)=inf{𝒟⁡(f):f∈𝒫k​with​‖f−μ​f‖L2​(μ)=1}​.{\rm gap}_{k}(G,\alpha)=\inf\left\{\mathcal{D}(f):f\in\mathscr{P}_{k}\ \text{with}\ \|f-\mu f\|_{L^{2}(\mu)}=1\right\}\;\text{.}

Our main finding here is that gap⁡(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha) and gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha) are comparable on any underlying geometry, up to a universal factor, essentially depending only on α\alpha.

Theorem 1.1 (KMP).

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

(1.7) γKMP​(G,α)​gap1​(G,α)≤gap⁡(G,α)≤gap1​(G,α)​,\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

where

(1.8) γKMP​(G,α)≔α2,min1+α2,min​(1+1|α|)​,\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\coloneqq\frac{\alpha_{2,\rm min}}{1+\alpha_{2,\rm min}}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\right)\;\text{,}\;\;

with

(1.9) α2,min=α2,min(G,α)≔minx,y:cx​y>0{αx+αy}.\alpha_{2,\rm min}=\alpha_{2,\rm min}(G,\alpha)\coloneqq\min_{x,y\,:\,c_{xy}>0}\left\{\alpha_{x}+\alpha_{y}\right\}\;\text{.}

Given the relation in (1.5) (which we will later prove in greater generality), the upper bound in (1.7) is clearly not surprising; it is the lower bound that actually constitutes the main result of the theorem. However, taken together, they offer a clearer picture of the sharpness of our bounds. Indeed, one always has γKMP​(G,α)∈(0,1)\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\in(0,1), as well as

(1.10) 2​αmin1+2​αmin​(1+1|α|)≤γKMP​(G,α)≤2​αmax1+2​αmax​(1+1|α|)​,\frac{2\alpha_{\rm min}}{1+2\alpha_{\rm min}}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\right)\leq\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\leq\frac{2\alpha_{\rm max}}{1+2\alpha_{\rm max}}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\right)\;\text{,}\;\;

where αmin≔minx∈V⁡αx\alpha_{\rm min}\coloneqq\min_{x\in V}\alpha_{x} and αmax≔maxx∈V⁡αx\alpha_{\rm max}\coloneqq\max_{x\in V}\alpha_{x}. Observe that both bounds in (1.10) do not depend on GG. As a consequence of (1.10), γKMP​(G,α)≈1\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\approx 1 (resp. 2n\frac{2}{n}) as αmin→∞\alpha_{\rm min}\to\infty (resp. αmax→0\alpha_{\rm max}\to 0 and αminαmax≈1\frac{\alpha_{\rm min}}{\alpha_{\rm max}}\approx 1). Finally, remark that γKMP​(G,α)\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha) can be much better than its lower bound in (1.10), whenever only a few isolated vertices x∈Vx\in V register αx→0\alpha_{x}\to 0.

Remark that working with gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha) instead of gap⁡(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha) offers a significant advantage: as we will see, gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha) admits a natural interpretation as the spectral gap of a random walk on a weighted graph. For such an object, a range of efficient estimation techniques from the theory of Markov chains and graph theory are available, and in some cases, even explicit formulas can be derived. This is precisely the case when αx≡const.=α^>0\alpha_{x}\equiv\text{const.}=\hat{\alpha}>0 and GG is either the complete graph or the segment. Comparing these explicit formulas with the KMP’s spectral gap identities in [CCL03, CLL20] allow us to assess the sharpness of Theorem 1.1 (Section 5.1.1): in the complete-graph case, the lower bound in (1.7) becomes an identity; on the segment, the upper bound is saturated whenever α^≥1\hat{\alpha}\geq 1.

1.2. Proof strategy and hidden parameter model

As already mentioned, prior to our work, spectral gap lower bounds for the KMP model have been established on the complete graph and on the segment. In particular, the first setting—corresponding to the mean-field scenario, much explored in kinetic theory—is now fully covered [Jan01, CCL03, Cap08]. In a nutshell, the common ingredient of all these proofs is a recursive argument on nn, the size of the graph, at the level of Dirichlet forms. This strategy, originated from Lu-Yau’s martingale method [LY93] and which proved to be extremely efficient and flexible to generalizations in the mean-field setup [CCL14, Sas15, CPT25], does not admit a sharp counterpart on arbitrary underlying geometries, especially in absence of symmetries.

Instead, we follow an alternative, equally established, route due to Chen and Wang [CW97] to bound from below eigenvalues of Markov generators, thus, spectral gaps of reversible processes. In essence, their proof goes as follows. Let λ>0\lambda>0 be an eigenvalue of −ℒ-\mathcal{L} associated to the eigenfunction ff satisfying μ​f=0\mu f=0, and (𝒮t)t≥0(\mathcal{S}_{t})_{t\geq 0} its corresponding semigroup. Then, one has, for any η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega and t>0t>0,

(1.11) |e−λ​t​f​(η)|=ﬁ​𝒮t​f​(η)=|𝒮t​f​(η)−μ​𝒮t​f|≤∫Ωμ⁡(d​η′)​|𝒮t​f​(η)−𝒮t​f​(η′)|​,\lvert e^{-\lambda t}f(\eta)\rvert=\char 12\relax{\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta)}=\lvert\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta)-\mu\mathcal{S}_{t}f\rvert\leq{\int_{\Omega}\mu({\rm d}\eta^{\prime})\lvert\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta)-\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta^{\prime})\rvert}\;\text{,}\;\;

and the task is to bound the right-hand side by C​e−ϱ​tCe^{-\varrho t}, for all t>0t>0 large enough and some constants C,ϱ>0C,\varrho>0 not depending on t>0t>0. Provided that f⁡(η)≠0f(\eta)\neq 0, taking the logarithm on both sides and sending t→∞t\to\infty would yield the lower bound λ≥ϱ\lambda\geq\varrho.

In fact, the crucial estimate

(1.12) ∫Ωμ⁡(d​η′)​|𝒮t​f​(η)−𝒮t​f​(η′)|≤C​e−ϱ​t\int_{\Omega}\mu({\rm d}\eta^{\prime})\lvert\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta)-\mathcal{S}_{t}f(\eta^{\prime})\rvert\leq Ce^{-\varrho t}

is derived in two main steps, see, e.g., [Che05, Theorem 2.42]:

  1. (1)

    Find a bounded nonnegative function 𝔡\mathfrak{d} on Ω×Ω\Omega\times\Omega controlling |f⁡(⋅)−f⁡(⋅)|\lvert f({\,\cdot\,})-f({\,\cdot\,})\rvert, that is,

    (1.13) supη,η′∈Ω|f⁡(η)−f⁡(η′)|𝔡⁡(η,η′)≤C1​,for some​C1>0​.\sup_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\Omega}\frac{\lvert f(\eta)-f(\eta^{\prime})\rvert}{\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})}\leq C_{1}\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{for some}\ C_{1}>0\;\text{.}

    Clearly, this forces 𝔡⁡(η,η)=0\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta)=0 for all η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega.

  2. (2)

    Find a Markovian coupling ~​𝒮t\tilde{}\mathcal{S}_{t} of two copies of 𝒮t\mathcal{S}_{t} under which 𝔡\mathfrak{d} decays exponentially fast, i.e., there exists ϱ>0\varrho>0 satisfying, for all t>0t>0 and η,η′∈Ω\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\Omega,

    (1.14) ~​𝒮t​𝔡​(η,η′)≤e−ϱ​t​𝔡​(η,η′)​.\tilde{}\mathcal{S}_{t}\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})\leq e^{-\varrho t}\,\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})\;\text{.}

    In particular, when 𝔡\mathfrak{d} is the pp-th power of a distance on Ω\Omega, (1.14) gives a pp-Wasserstein (with respect to 𝔡1/p\mathfrak{d}^{1/p}) bound.

These two estimates yield (1.12) with C=C1​supη,η′∈Ω𝔡⁡(η,η′)>0C=C_{1}\sup_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\Omega}\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})>0. The challenge is, thus, to devise such a (i) control function and (ii) coupling.

1.2.1. Chen-Wang’s approach for KMP{\rm KMP}

Within the context of the KMP model, this program has been successfully carried out, for α≡const.\alpha\equiv{\rm const.}, on the complete graph [Hau16] and on the segment [GKS12]. Both works employ the so-called grand-coupling: let the two configurations evolve as in (1.1) by simultaneously updating the same edge and sharing the same UU. As for 𝔡\mathfrak{d}, [Hau16] considers the squared Euclidean distance on Ω\Omega:

(1.15) 𝔡⁡(η,η′)=d​(η,η′)2≔∑x∈V(ηx−ηx′)2​.\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})=d(\eta,\eta^{\prime})^{2}\coloneqq\sum_{x\in V}\left(\eta_{x}-\eta_{x}^{\prime}\right)^{2}\;\text{.}

It is instructive to check what [Hau16] yields on a general graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}): letting ~​ℒ\tilde{}\mathcal{L} denote the generator of the semigroup (~​𝒮t)t≥0(\tilde{}\mathcal{S}_{t})_{t\geq 0}, by following the steps in the proof of [Hau16, Theorem 1], one gets (recall that here we assume α≡α^>0\alpha\equiv\hat{\alpha}>0)

(1.16) ~​ℒ​d​(η,η′)2=−α^4​α^+2∑x,y∈Vx≠ycx​y{(ηx−ηx′)−(ηy−ηy′)}2+12​α^+1∑x,y∈Vx≠ycx​y(ηx−ηx′)(ηy−ηy′).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \tilde{}\mathcal{L}\,d(\eta,\eta^{\prime})^{2}&=-\frac{\hat{\alpha}}{4\hat{\alpha}+2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in V\\ x\neq y\end{subarray}}c_{xy}\left\{\left(\eta_{x}-\eta_{x}^{\prime}\right)-\left(\eta_{y}-\eta_{y}^{\prime}\right)\right\}^{2}\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2\hat{\alpha}+1}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in V\\ x\neq y\end{subarray}}c_{xy}\left(\eta_{x}-\eta_{x}^{\prime}\right)\left(\eta_{y}-\eta_{y}^{\prime}\right)\;\text{.}\end{aligned}

On the complete graph, that is, when cx​y≡1n>0c_{xy}\equiv\frac{1}{n}>0, both summations on the right-hand side can be reduced to a negative constant—depending on |V|=n|V|=n and α^\hat{\alpha}—times d​(η,η′)2d(\eta,\eta^{\prime})^{2}. Here, one crucially uses that ∑y≠xcx​y​(ηy−ηy′)=−1n​(ηx−ηx′)\sum_{y\neq x}c_{xy}\left(\eta_{y}-\eta_{y}^{\prime}\right)=-\frac{1}{n}\left(\eta_{x}-\eta_{x}^{\prime}\right). Recalling that ~​ℒ​~​𝒮t=dd​t​~​𝒮t\tilde{}\mathcal{L}\tilde{}\mathcal{S}_{t}=\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\tilde{}\mathcal{S}_{t}, integrating this infinitesimal identity yields the desired exponential contraction as in (1.14). Interestingly, the spectral gap lower bound obtained in this way matches the exact value [CCL03, Cap08].

When GG is not the complete graph, this simplification breaks down. In particular, while the first expression is nonpositive and eventually comparable to d​(η,η′)2d(\eta,\eta^{\prime})^{2}, the second line in (1.16) does not have, in general, a prescribed sign. This represents the main obstacle in making this strategy work on arbitrary graphs, as different couplings and control functions need to be constructed.

On the segment, for instance, [GKS12] overcomes this issue by replacing the squared distance of η,η′∈Ω\eta,\eta^{\prime}\in\Omega in (1.15) with that of their height functions, namely,

(1.17) 𝔡⁡(η,η′)=∑x∈V(∑y≤xηy−∑y≤xηy′)2​.\mathfrak{d}(\eta,\eta^{\prime})=\sum_{x\in V}\bigg(\sum_{y\leq x}\eta_{y}-\sum_{y\leq x}\eta_{y}^{\prime}\bigg)^{2}\;\text{.}

This choice is clearly effective only on one-dimensional graphs. For more details, we refer the interested reader to [GKS12, Proposition 2.6], as well as to [CLL20, LP25], which determine the spectral gap for some choices of α\alpha, with αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1.

1.2.2. KMP{\rm KMP}’s hidden parameter model

Our way to tackle this difficulty on arbitrary graphs is to apply the same strategy, not to the KMP process itself, but to a recently discovered dual process [DMFG24] (see also [GRT25]): the KMP hidden parameter model. Before discussing the details, we begin with a few preliminary remarks.

Recall that ℒ\mathcal{L} leaves 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k}, the space of polynomials of degree kk in the η\eta-variables, invariant. More specifically, let f∈𝒫kf\in\mathscr{P}_{k}, and represent it as

(1.18) f(η)=∑x1,…,xk∈Vψ(x1,…,xk)ηx1⋯ηxk,η∈Ω,f(\eta)=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V}\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\eta_{x_{1}}\cdots\eta_{x_{k}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\eta\in\Omega\;\text{,}\;\;

for some symmetric function ψ:Vk→ℝ\psi:V^{k}\to\mathbb{R}. Since ℒ\mathcal{L} is linear and η\eta vary in Ω\Omega, the action of ℒ\mathcal{L} on f=f⁡(η)f=f(\eta) translates into one on the coefficients ψ=ψ⁡(x1,…,xk)\psi=\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}), that is, there exists a linear operator LL on ℝVk\mathbb{R}^{V^{k}} satisfying, for all η∈Ω\eta\in\Omega,

(1.19) ℒf(η)=∑x1,…,xk∈Vψ(x1,…,xk)ℒηx1⋯ηxk=∑x1,…,xk∈VLψ(x1,…,xk)ηx1⋯ηxk.\mathcal{L}f(\eta)=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V}\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\mathcal{L}\,{\eta_{x_{1}}\cdots\eta_{x_{k}}}=\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V}L\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\eta_{x_{1}}\cdots\eta_{x_{k}}\;\text{.}

As we shall see in Section 3.1, and as is well-known, LL has a probabilistic interpretation in terms of a particle dynamics, and the identity above is an instance of an intertwining relation. What matters for us now is that, since any eigenfunction of −ℒ-\mathcal{L} must be a polynomial, this implies that, if ff in (1.18) solves ℒ​f=−λ​f\mathcal{L}f=-\lambda f, then so do its coefficients, i.e.,

(1.20) L​ψ=−λ​ψ​.L\psi=-\lambda\psi\;\text{.}

Exploiting this equivalent reformulation of the eigenvalue equation for KMP seems as hard as the one we started from. Instead, we combine the eigenfunction ψ\psi in (1.20) with different variables, as follows

(1.21) g(θ)≔∑x1,…,xk∈Vαx1⋯xkψ(x1,…,xk)θx1⋯θxk,θ∈[0,1]V,g(\theta)\coloneqq\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\in V}\alpha_{x_{1}\cdots x_{k}}\,\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\theta_{x_{1}}\cdots\theta_{x_{k}}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\theta\in[0,1]^{V}\;\text{,}\;\;

where αx1⋯xk≔αx1(αx2+𝟙x2(x1))⋯(αxk+∑j<k𝟙xk(xj))\alpha_{x_{1}\cdots x_{k}}\coloneqq\alpha_{x_{1}}\left(\alpha_{x_{2}}+\mathds{1}_{x_{2}}(x_{1})\right)\cdots(\alpha_{x_{k}}+\sum_{j<k}\mathds{1}_{x_{k}}(x_{j})). This seemingly marginal change turns out to be surprisingly effective.

The action of the linear operator LL on ψ\psi translates into a new one on the θ\theta-variables, which we call ℒ\mathscr{L}: for all θ∈[0,1]V\theta\in[0,1]^{V},

(1.22) ∑x1,…,xkαx1⋯xkLψ(x1,…,xk)θx1⋯θxk\displaystyle\sum_{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}}\alpha_{x_{1}\cdots x_{k}}\,L\psi(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\,\theta_{x_{1}}\cdots\theta_{x_{k}} =ℒ​g​(θ)​.\displaystyle=\mathscr{L}g(\theta)\;\text{.}

Hence, if ψ\psi solves (1.20), then ℒ​g=−λ​g\mathscr{L}g=-\lambda g. Altogether, we obtained

(1.23) ℒ​f=−λ​f⇒L​ψ=−λ​ψ⇒ℒ​g=−λ​g​.\mathcal{L}f=-\lambda f\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad L\psi=-\lambda\psi\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\mathscr{L}g=-\lambda g\;\text{.}

The operator ℒ\mathscr{L} just introduced turns out to be the infinitesimal generator of the hidden parameter model of the KMP. Therefore, letting (𝒮t)t≥0(\mathscr{S}_{t})_{t\geq 0} be its Markov semigroup, by the same reasoning as above, we obtain a lower bound for λ\lambda if we prove

(1.24) |e−λ​t​g​(θ)|=|𝒮t​g​(θ)|≤C​e−ϱ​t​,\lvert e^{-\lambda t}g(\theta)\rvert=\lvert\mathscr{S}_{t}g(\theta)\rvert\leq Ce^{-\varrho t}\;\text{,}\;\;

for all t>0t>0 large enough, and for some C,ϱ>0C,\varrho>0 and θ∈[0,1]V\theta\in[0,1]^{V} satisfying g⁡(θ)≠0g(\theta)\neq 0.

For the proof of the upper bound in (1.24), we exploit the probabilistic interpretation of ℒ\mathscr{L} and 𝒮t\mathscr{S}_{t}. On a given graph, KMP and its hidden parameter model θ\theta evolve according to the same stochastic mechanisms: edges are selected at the same rate, and an analogous beta-distributed random variable UU is sampled. However, the resulting θ\theta-configuration is not obtained from the update rule in (1.1); instead, it transitions from (θx,θy)(\theta_{x},\theta_{y}) to

(1.25) (U​θx+(1−U)​θy,U​θx+(1−U)​θy)​.(U\theta_{x}+(1-U)\theta_{y},U\theta_{x}+(1-U)\theta_{y})\;\text{.}

Remark that (1.25) describes a dynamics that:

  • •

    does not, in general, conserve the total mass |θ|=∑x∈Vθx|\theta|=\sum_{x\in V}\theta_{x};

  • •

    satisfies the maximum principle: if maxx∈V⁡θx≤1\max_{x\in V}\theta_{x}\leq 1 holds at time t=0t=0, then this holds true almost surely at any later time;

  • •

    leaves constant configurations invariant; moreover, if GG is connected, these are the only invariant ones.

This last feature plays a crucial role in our analysis. While having equilibrium states supported only on constant configurations may appear to introduce a degeneracy, it is in fact beneficial: convergence to equilibrium for the hidden parameter model requires no coupling, but only a control over spatial fluctuations. The decay of these fluctuations is quantified by the following L2L^{2}-estimate (here, π=(πx)x∈V\pi=(\pi_{x})_{x\in V} with πx=αx|α|\pi_{x}=\frac{\alpha_{x}}{|\alpha|}): for all t≥0t\geq 0,

(1.26) (𝒮t​Varπ)​(θ)≤e−ϱ​t​Varπ​(θ)​,(\mathscr{S}_{t}{\rm Var}_{\pi})(\theta)\leq e^{-\varrho t}\,{\rm Var}_{\pi}(\theta)\;\text{,}\;\;

with θ↦Varπ​(θ)=‖θ−π​θ‖L2​(π)2\theta\mapsto{\rm Var}_{\pi}(\theta)=\|\theta-\pi\theta\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}^{2} being the suitable control function for kk-degree eigenfunctions, k≥2k\geq 2 (Section 4.1). Ultimately, establishing estimates as in (1.26) boils down to a straightforward second moment computation (Section 4.2). Remarkably, these estimates are broadly applicable: they are graph- and coupling-independent, and yield tight bounds across a wide class of processes.

1.3. Generalizations: HP & IEM, and beyond reversibility

The strategy outlined for bounding KMP’s spectral gap turns out to be much more general, yet, surprisingly sharp. Indeed, it covers all conservative stochastic exchange models that are reversible, and that come with a “degenerate” hidden parameter model. In certain instances, the spectral gap estimates derived through this approach actually become exact identities, on any graph.

Stochastic exchange models which are conservative and admit a hidden parameter model take a rather general form, see (2.1): transitions correspond to stochastic mappings, with the corresponding rates being independent of the process’ state. In contrast, reversibility imposes a specific form on the transition rates.

1.3.1. Harmonic process & immediate exchange model

We mainly consider two notable examples in this class: the harmonic process (HP) [FG22, FFG23] and the immediate exchange model (IEM) [Kat15, GRS16]. A rough description of their dynamics on (G,α)(G,\alpha) goes as follows (see Sections 2 and 5 for a complete description): HP’s transitions go from (ηx,ηy)(\eta_{x},\eta_{y}) to

(1.27) (U​ηx,(1−U)​ηx+ηy)​,(U\eta_{x},(1-U)\eta_{x}+\eta_{y})\;\text{,}\;\;

where the random UU takes the value u∈(0,1)u\in(0,1) with an “infinitesimal rate”, namely, cx​y​(1−u)−1​uαx−1​d​uc_{xy}\left(1-u\right)^{-1}u^{\alpha_{x}-1}\,{\rm d}u; IEM’s updates result in replacing, at rate cx​y≥0c_{xy}\geq 0, (ηx,ηy)(\eta_{x},\eta_{y}) with

(1.28) (U​ηx+(1−V)​ηy,(1−U)​ηx+V​ηy)​,(U\eta_{x}+(1-V)\eta_{y},(1-U)\eta_{x}+V\eta_{y})\;\text{,}\;\;

where U,V∈(0,1)U,V\in(0,1) are independent and distributed as

(1.29) U∼Beta⁡(αx−κ,κ)​,V∼Beta⁡(αy−κ,κ)​.U\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{x}-\kappa,\kappa)\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad V\sim{\rm Beta}(\alpha_{y}-\kappa,\kappa)\;\text{.}

Here, κ∈(0,αmin)\kappa\in(0,\alpha_{\rm min}) is an additional fixed parameter of the model.

HP and IEM fall into our general class of stochastic exchange models. Furthermore, because both models admit μ∼Dir⁡(α)\mu\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha) as a reversible measure, the spectral gap decomposition in (1.4)–(1.6) holds analogously for both models. In the following theorems, we specialize the main results from Section 2.3 to the context of HP and IEM. Observe that, although we simply write gap⁡(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha) and gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha) as in Theorem 1.1, these quantities depend, in general, on the model considered. All throughout, a∧b≔min⁡{a,b}a\wedge b\coloneqq\min\{a,b\}, a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R}.

Theorem 1.2 (HP).

For all graphs G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}) and weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V},

(1.30) (1∧γHP​(G,α))​gap1​(G,α)≤gap⁡(G,α)≤gap1​(G,α)​,\left(1\wedge\gamma_{\rm HP}(G,\alpha)\right){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}(G,\alpha)\leq{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)\;\text{,}\;\;

where

(1.31) γHP(G,α)≔minx,y:cx​y>0{αxαx+1+αyαy+1}(1+1|α|).\gamma_{\rm HP}(G,\alpha)\coloneqq\min_{x,y\,:\,c_{xy}>0}\left\{\frac{\alpha_{x}}{\alpha_{x}+1}+\frac{\alpha_{y}}{\alpha_{y}+1}\right\}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\right)\;\text{.}
Theorem 1.3 (IEM).

For all G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V}, and κ∈(0,αmin)\kappa\in(0,\alpha_{\rm min}),

(1.32) (1∧γIEM​(G,α,κ))​gap1​(G,α,κ)≤gap⁡(G,α,κ)≤gap1​(G,α,κ)​,\left(1\wedge\gamma_{\rm IEM}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\right){\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\leq{\rm gap}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\leq{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\;\text{,}\;\;

where

(1.33) γIEM(G,α,κ)≔minx,y:cx​y>0{αx−καx+1+αy−καy+1}(1+1|α|).\gamma_{\rm IEM}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\coloneqq\min_{x,y\,:\,c_{xy}>0}\left\{\frac{\alpha_{x}-\kappa}{\alpha_{x}+1}+\frac{\alpha_{y}-\kappa}{\alpha_{y}+1}\right\}\left(1+\frac{1}{|\alpha|}\right)\;\text{.}

Strikingly, if αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 (resp. αmin≥1+2​κ\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1+2\kappa), then the bounds in (1.30) (resp. (1.32)) are actually identities, that is, gap⁡(G,α)=gap1​(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha). Whenever this identity does not hold, we prove that the lower bounds are attained on specific graphs; see Sections 5.2.1 and 5.3.1. Observe that the regime αmin≥1\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1 corresponds to log-concavity of μ∼Dir⁡(α)\mu\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha).

Finally, let us note that the homogeneous HP model on the segment is known to be integrable [FG22]. Consequently, all eigenvalues of the HP model in this specific setting are, at least in principle, explicitly computable. However, no results on the spectral gap of either of these two models were available, in any geometry, prior to the inequalities and identities stated in Theorems 1.2 and 1.3.

1.3.2. Beyond non-degeneracy and reversibility

All three models discussed earlier share the key feature of admitting a non-degenerate reversible measure. These two properties are instrumental in applying the spectral theorem to self-adjoint generators, which in turn guarantees that the polynomial eigenvalues we compute actually saturate the corresponding L2L^{2}-spectrum. However, one of the main strengths of our approach is that neither non-degeneracy nor reversibility is essential for obtaining sharp eigenvalue estimates. Indeed, we identify a broad family of stochastic exchange models—with update rules as in (1.28), see (2.1)—for which our method remains effective even in the absence of these assumptions, thus significantly extending the range of models to which our spectral analysis applies.

To begin with, our strategy remains effective in degenerate settings, where the invariant measure is singular, that is, μ=δω\mu=\delta_{\omega}, for some ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega. This occurs, for example, in certain averaging-type models in which one imposes the requirement

(1.34) V=1−ωxωy​(1−U)V=1-\frac{\omega_{x}}{\omega_{y}}\left(1-U\right)

at each update in (1.28). In such cases, the system converges to the configuration ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega; when ω≡1n\omega\equiv\frac{1}{n}, the above requirement becomes U≡VU\equiv V.

In these settings, no meaningful L2L^{2}-space compatible with ℒ\mathcal{L} can be defined; nevertheless, our method remains applicable and yields explicit lower bounds on eigenvalues associated with polynomial observables. These bounds are not merely formal. As shown in Section 3.1, for each integer k≥1k\geq 1, a stochastic exchange model naturally gives rise to a kk-particle interacting system. In the specific case described in (1.34), it is straightforward to check that these particle systems always admit a fully supported reversible measure. Consequently, our eigenvalue estimates yield lower bounds on the spectral gap of the corresponding particle systems, uniformly in the number of particles, k≥1k\geq 1. We note that the averaging model with U≡ωxωx+ωyU\equiv\frac{\omega_{x}}{\omega_{x}+\omega_{y}} in (1.34) was considered in [QS23].

Even more significantly, our approach yields meaningful lower bounds on the real part of eigenvalues for a broad class of non-reversible stochastic exchange models and their associated particle systems. This class includes models with asymmetric updates, as well as models arising in econophysics, where the conserved quantity is interpreted as wealth and the dynamics incorporates a nonzero saving propensity. As shown in [CRR14], such models are intrinsically non-reversible.

1.3.3. Open systems

Hidden parameter models for the KMP and the HP recently sparked attention within the context of open systems, in contact with external reservoirs, providing a useful alternative description of the corresponding non-equilibrium steady states [DMFG24, CFG+24, CFF+25, GRT25]. Each of our general stochastic exchange models admits a non-conservative counterpart, with suitably chosen boundary-driven dynamics. The polynomial-eigenvalue analysis presented in [KS24a, Section 6] for a related open diffusion process can be similarly applied to our models, yielding analogous results—specifically, that the lowest polynomial eigenvalue is attained by linear functions. For the sake of brevity, we will not discuss this setting in any detail.

1.4. Organization of the paper

The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we introduce a general class of stochastic exchange models, discuss some of their basic properties, and present our main results on eigenvalue and spectral gap estimates. Section 3 presents definitions and main properties of three Markov processes related to our stochastic exchange models. Section 4 contains the core of the proof of the main results from Section 2. Section 5 presents a detailed discussion of the three models introduced so far and illustrates our main results by applying them to prove Theorems 1.1–1.3.

2. General setting and main results

The following assumption will be enough to ensure uniqueness of invariant measures for our stochastic exchange models.

Assumption 2.5.

Remark 2.6.

By confronting (2.18) with (2.19), we have sx​y≤rx​ys_{xy}\leq r_{xy} for all distinct x,y∈Vx,y\in V. Therefore, Assumption 2.5 implies irreducibility of RW and, thus, the existence of a unique positive invariant measure π=(πx)x∈V∈𝒫⁡(V)\pi=(\pi_{x})_{x\in V}\in\mathcal{P}(V) for RW, that is,

Proposition 2.7 (Invariant measure).

Under Assumptions 2.3 and 2.5, the stochastic exchange model on Ω\Omega described by (2.1) admits a unique invariant measure.

Since Ω\Omega is compact, the existence part of this proposition was already part of Proposition 2.4; the uniqueness part will be proved in Section 3.1, see Corollary 3.3.

2.3. Main results

In this section, Assumptions 2.3 and 2.5 are in force.

In view of Assumption 2.3 and Proposition 2.4, ℒ\mathcal{L}, restricted to the finite-dimensional space 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k} of kk-degree polynomials in η\eta, is a well-defined linear operator. Hence, −ℒ|𝒫k-\mathcal{L}\rvert_{\mathscr{P}_{k}} admits a decomposition in (possibly complex) eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. In particular, by (2.18), when k=1k=1, such eigenvalues coincide with those of the generator of RW with rates (rx​y)x,y∈V(r_{xy})_{x,y\in V}. Assumption 2.5 and Remark 2.6 ensure that only one of such eigenvalues is zero. Any other RW-eigenvalue λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} satisfies (see, e.g., [SC97, Theorem 2.1.7])

(2.22) gapRW​(ℒ)≤Re⁡(λ)​,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L})\leq{\rm Re}(\lambda)\;\text{,}\;\;

where gapRW​(ℒ)>0{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L})>0 is the RW’s spectral gap, that is,

(2.23) gapRW​(ℒ)≔inf{ℰRW​(ψ):ψ∈ℝV​with​‖ψ−π​ψ‖L2​(π)=1}​,{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L})\coloneqq\inf\left\{\mathcal{E}_{\rm RW}(\psi):\psi\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\ \text{with}\ \|\psi-\pi\psi\|_{L^{2}(\pi)}=1\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;

with ℰRW\mathcal{E}_{\rm RW} being the RW’s Dirichlet form:

(2.24) ℰRW​(ψ)≔12​∑x,y∈Vπx​y​(ψ⁡(y)−ψ⁡(x))2​,πx​y≔πx​rx​y+πy​ry​x2​.\mathcal{E}_{\rm RW}(\psi)\coloneqq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{x,y\in V}\pi_{xy}\left(\psi(y)-\psi(x)\right)^{2}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\pi_{xy}\coloneqq\frac{\pi_{x}r_{xy}+\pi_{y}r_{yx}}{2}\;\text{.}

The bound in (2.22) always holds true for eigenvalues of −ℒ|𝒫k-\mathcal{L}\rvert_{\mathscr{P}_{k}}, for k=1k=1. Our main result provides a related bound for all k≥2k\geq 2. Its proof is the content of Section 4.

Fix k≥2k\geq 2. Let λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} be an eigenvalue of −ℒ|𝒫k-\mathcal{L}\rvert_{\mathscr{P}_{k}}, but not of ℒ|𝒫k−1\mathcal{L}\rvert_{\mathscr{P}_{k-1}}. Then,

with πx​y\pi_{xy} given as in (2.24) (see also (2.18)), and

While χx​y\chi_{xy} is proportional to πx+πy\pi_{x}+\pi_{y}, σx​y\sigma_{xy} is comparable to (πx+πy)2(\pi_{x}+\pi_{y})^{2}. In many examples, this translates into σx​y≪χx​y\sigma_{xy}\ll\chi_{xy} in the large-graph limit |V|=n→∞|V|=n\to\infty.

The above theorem does not require any reversibility, nor a specific form of the invariant measure. At this level of generality, eigenvalues of the infinite-dimensional operator −ℒ-\mathcal{L} do not necessarily exhaust its spectrum, which, in turn, may depend on the functional space on which −ℒ-\mathcal{L} acts on.

Our next result fully exploits Theorem 2.8, showing that when the process is reversible with respect to a non-degenerate Dirichlet distribution, the L2L^{2}-spectrum coincides with the set of polynomial eigenvalues. Consequently, the estimates in Theorem 2.8 yield explicit bounds on the spectral gap.

where gapRW​(ℒ){\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L}) and γ⁡(ℒ)\gamma(\mathcal{L}) are given in (2.23) and (2.26), respectively.

The proofs of the last two theorems are deferred to Section 4. In Section 5, we apply them to the three models discussed in Theorems 1.1–1.3.

2.3.1. Aldous’ spectral gap identities

Theorem 2.11 provides both upper and lower bounds for gap⁡(ℒ){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L}) solely in terms of

(2.30) gapRW​(ℒ)and1∧γ⁡(ℒ)​.{\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L})\qquad\text{and}\qquad 1\wedge\gamma(\mathcal{L})\;\text{.}

In particular, whenever γ⁡(ℒ)≥1\gamma(\mathcal{L})\geq 1, the spectral gap of the stochastic exchange model coincides with that of the corresponding random walk on the same graph. This striking dimensionality reduction holding for any underlying graph GG is reminiscent of the celebrated Aldous’ spectral gap conjecture—later resolved by Caputo, Liggett, and Richthammer [CLR10]—which established a similar identity between the spectral gaps of the interchange process, the symmetric exclusion process, and the associated random walk.

Somewhat surprisingly, such reductions have recently emerged in a number of structurally diverse models, see [HS19, QS23, Sal23, Sal24, KS24b, KS24a]. Consequently, identifying conditions that ensure γ⁡(ℒ)≥1\gamma(\mathcal{L})\geq 1 offers a practical criterion for verifying an analogue of Aldous’ spectral gap identity within this broad class of stochastic exchange models reversible with respect to a Dirichlet distribution. In this setting, the relatively explicit expression of γ⁡(ℒ)\gamma(\mathcal{L}) given in (2.26) allows us to derive, after a simple manipulation, the following effective criterion.

Corollary 2.14.

In the context of Theorem 2.11, we have gap​(ℒ)=gapRW​(ℒ){\rm gap}(\mathcal{L})={\rm gap}_{\rm RW}(\mathcal{L}) as soon as

(2.31) ∫[0,1]2[βx​y​(𝑑u,𝑑v)+βy​x​(𝑑v,𝑑u)]​(1−u)​(2​u−1)≥0​,for all distinct​x,y∈V​.\int_{[0,1]^{2}}\left[\beta_{xy}({\rm d}u,{\rm d}v)+\beta_{yx}({\rm d}v,{\rm d}u)\right]\left(1-u\right)(2u-1)\geq 0\;\text{,}\;\;\quad\text{for all distinct}\ x,y\in V\;\text{.}

3. Particle systems, intertwinings, and hidden parameter models

In this section, we introduce three families of Markov processes, all closely related to the stochastic exchange models described in Section 2.1: an interacting particle system, its time reversal, and the hidden parameter model. Here, we collect their most relevant properties, as well as duality and intertwining relations, of independent interest and all instrumental to the proof of our main results.

3.1. Particle systems and forward intertwinings

Particle systems arise naturally from the stochastic exchange models introduced in Section 2.1, and turn out to be convenient to work with. Informally, they can be described as follows.

Let (η⁡(t))t≥0(\eta(t))_{t\geq 0} be a fixed realization of the process with generator ℒ\mathcal{L} in (2.1). Recall that, for any time t≥0t\geq 0, η⁡(t)\eta(t) is a probability distribution on VV. Consider k≥1k\geq 1 particle positions X1​(0),…,Xk​(0)X_{1}(0),\ldots,X_{k}(0) on VV, being i.i.d. and such that Xi​(0)∼η⁡(0)∈ΩX_{i}(0)\sim\eta(0)\in\Omega. Given this initial condition, let particles move at each η\eta-update: assuming that there is a first update at time t>0t>0 involving the vertices x,y∈Vx,y\in V and fractions u,v∈[0,1]u,v\in[0,1], then set

(3.1) Xi​(t)={xifXi(t−)=x,w/ prob.u∨ifXi(t−)=y,w/ prob. 1−v,yifXi(t−)=y,w/ prob.v∨ifXi(t−)=x,w/ prob. 1−u,Xi​(t−)else​,X_{i}(t)=\begin{cases}x&\text{if}\ X_{i}(t^{-})=x,\ \text{w/ prob.}\ u\ \vee\text{if}\ X_{i}(t^{-})=y,\ \text{w/ prob.}\ 1-v\;\text{,}\\ y&\text{if}\ X_{i}(t^{-})=y,\ \text{w/ prob.}\ v\ \vee\text{if}\ X_{i}(t^{-})=x,\ \text{w/ prob.}\ 1-u\;\text{,}\\ X_{i}(t^{-})&\text{else}\;\text{,}\end{cases}

and this independently over i=1,…,ki=1,\ldots,k. This Markovian dynamics clearly generates, at any later time t>0t>0, kk independent samples from η⁡(t)∈Ω\eta(t)\in\Omega. This is true for a given realization of (η⁡(t))t≥0(\eta(t))_{t\geq 0}, that is, in a quenched sense. The main point is that the annealed process obtained through an averaging over all updates introduces a dependence over the particles’ evolution, although the particle system preserves the Markov property. We now formalize these ideas.

Fix an integer k≥1k\geq 1. Recall from (1.18) the general form of a kk-degree polynomial f∈𝒫kf\in\mathscr{P}_{k} in the η\eta-variables. Letting (ℕ0≔{0,1,2,…}\mathbb{N}_{0}\coloneqq\left\{0,1,2,\ldots\right\})

3.2. Annihilation and creation operators

Fix an integer k≥1k\geq 1, and introduce the (particle) annihilation operator 𝔞:ℂΞk−1→ℂΞk\mathfrak{a}:\mathbb{C}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\to\mathbb{C}^{\Xi_{k}} (conventionally, Ξ0≡{∅}\Xi_{0}\equiv\left\{\emptyset\right\} and ℂΞ0≅ℂ\mathbb{C}^{\Xi_{0}}\cong\mathbb{C}), given by

(3.19) 𝔞​ψ​(ξ)≔∑x∈Vξx​ψ​(ξ−δx)​,ξ∈Ξk​,​ψ∈ℂΞk−1​.\mathfrak{a}\psi(\xi)\coloneqq\sum_{x\in V}\xi_{x}\,\psi(\xi-\delta_{x})\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\xi\in\Xi_{k}\;\text{,}\;\;\psi\in\mathbb{C}^{\Xi_{k-1}}\;\text{.}

Up to a normalization factor, 𝔞​ψ​(ξ)\mathfrak{a}\psi(\xi) is the average of the function ψ\psi after removing a particle uniformly at random from ξ\xi.

Our next result states that the particle system with generator LL commutes with this operation: removing a particle at the start and then evolving is the same (in law) as first evolving and then removing.

Proposition 3.5.

𝔞​L=L​𝔞\mathfrak{a}L=L\mathfrak{a}.

Proof (Sketch).

The proof goes either via a direct (but lengthy) computation, or via the observation that any subset of the kk “quenched” particles X1​(t),…,Xk​(t)X_{1}(t),\ldots,X_{k}(t) discussed at the beginning of Section 3.1 remains Markovian and evolves with the correct law. For an analogous statement, see, e.g., [CGR21] or [KS24b, Appendix]. ∎

3.3. Hidden parameter models and backward intertwinings

Given the generator ℒ\mathcal{L} in (2.1), ℒ\mathscr{L} in (2.5) is the corresponding hidden parameter model’s generator. Assumption 2.3 and an argument as in the proof of Proposition 2.4 guarantees that ℒ\mathscr{L} is a well-defined operator on polynomials on [0,1]V[0,1]^{V}, and uniquely identifies a Feller process (θ⁡(t))t≥0(\theta(t))_{t\geq 0} therein.

4. Proofs of main results

In this section, we prove Theorems 2.8 and 2.11. The first two subsections develop the two key steps of the proof strategy described in Section 1.2. The third subsection puts these two together, closing the proof of Theorem 2.8, while the final one is dedicated to the proof of Theorem 2.11.

4.4. Proof of Theorem 2.11

Fix α\alpha and μ∼Dir⁡(α)\mu\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha). We divide the proof of Theorem 2.11 into two parts: one for the main claim and the lower bound in (2.29), one for the upper bound in (2.29).

Proof of the lower bound in Theorem 2.11.

Since μ\mu is absolutely continuous with respect to the uniform measure on Ω\Omega, ℒ\mathcal{L} in (2.1), viewed as an operator on polynomials in 𝒫\mathscr{P}, is well-defined as an operator on equivalence classes in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu). Since ℒ\mathcal{L} leaves 𝒫k\mathscr{P}_{k}, k≥0k\geq 0, invariant, and is symmetric on the the dense subspace 𝒫⊂L2​(μ)\mathscr{P}\subset L^{2}(\mu), there exists a c.o.n.s.

(4.48) fk​j∈𝒫k,†​,k∈ℕ0​,​j=1,…,Nk≔|Ξk|−|Ξk−1|​,f_{kj}\in\mathscr{P}_{k,\dagger}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}\;\text{,}\;\;j=1,\ldots,N_{k}\coloneqq|\Xi_{k}|-|\Xi_{k-1}|\;\text{,}\;\;

in L2​(μ)L^{2}(\mu) of polynomial eigenfunctions for −ℒ-\mathcal{L}, all associated to real, nonnegative eigenvalues. Hence, −ℒ-\mathcal{L} is essentially self-adjoint [RS72, Theorem VIII.3], and the spectral theorem applies to its unique closed extension, ensuring a pure point spectrum. Theorem 2.8 yields the lower bound in (2.29). ∎

Remark 4.5.

Along the same lines of the proof above, it is not difficult to check that if ℒ\mathcal{L} admits μ∼Dir⁡(α)\mu\sim{\rm Dir}(\alpha) as a reversible measure, then LL is self-adjoint on L2​(μ^k)L^{2}(\widehat{\mu}_{k}), not only for k=1k=1, but for all k≥1k\geq 1.

The proof of the lower bound in Theorem 2.11 actually remains valid also when μ\mu is not a Dirichlet measure, but merely absolutely continuous on Ω\Omega.

5. Examples. Proofs of Theorems 1.1–1.3

We now discuss in more detail a few examples of reversible stochastic exchange model on an undirected weighted connected finite graph G=(V,(cx​y)x,y∈V)G=(V,(c_{xy})_{x,y\in V}), where cx​y=cy​x≥0c_{xy}=c_{yx}\geq 0 are symmetric conductances. Further, we fix some positive weights α=(αx)x∈V\alpha=(\alpha_{x})_{x\in V} attached to vertices. Given all this, we think of the rates βx​y\beta_{xy} and βy​x\beta_{yx} as being proportional to cx​y≥0c_{xy}\geq 0 and depending on αx,αy>0\alpha_{x},\alpha_{y}>0.

For all the models that we now consider, Assumptions 2.3 and 2.5 always hold true, and Dir⁡(α){\rm Dir}(\alpha) in (1.3) is their unique reversible measure; thus, Theorem 2.11 and Corollary 2.14 apply; see also Remark 2.12. Before entering their details, we mention that all computations below, although somewhat lengthy, are simple, merely based on the following standard identities involving the Gamma function: for all a,b>0a,b>0,

(5.1) ∫01ua−1​(1−u)b−1​𝑑u=Γ⁡(a)​Γ​(b)Γ⁡(a+b)​,Γ⁡(a+1)=a​Γ​(a)​.\int_{0}^{1}u^{a-1}\left(1-u\right)^{b-1}{\rm d}u=\frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad\Gamma(a+1)=a\Gamma(a)\;\text{.}

5.1. The Kipnis-Marchioro-Presutti model

Define, for all distinct x,y∈Vx,y\in V,

(5.2) βx​y​(d​u,d​v)=cx​y2​B​(αx,αy)​uαx−1​(1−u)αy−1​d​u​δ1−u​(d​v)​,\beta_{xy}({\rm d}u,{\rm d}v)=\frac{c_{xy}}{2\,{\rm B}(\alpha_{x},\alpha_{y})}u^{\alpha_{x}-1}\left(1-u\right)^{\alpha_{y}-1}{\rm d}u\,\delta_{1-u}({\rm d}v)\;\text{,}\;\;

where B⁡(αx,αy)=B⁡(αy,αx){\rm B}(\alpha_{x},\alpha_{y})={\rm B}(\alpha_{y},\alpha_{x}) is the Beta function (i.e., the normalization constant defined in (1.3) with V={x,y}V=\left\{x,y\right\}). These rates correspond to an edge heat-bath dynamics with respect to the Dirichlet distribution, possibly with edge and vertex inhomogeneities. Therefore, reversibility readily follows.

With this choice, the corresponding rr-rates read as (cf. (2.18))

and

where α2,min\alpha_{2,\rm min} is given in (1.9). This corresponds to the main claim in Theorem 1.1.

5.1.1. Sharpness for KMP{\rm KMP}

When αx≡α^>0\alpha_{x}\equiv\hat{\alpha}>0 is constant, for the KMP model we recover

(5.11) γKMP​(G,α)=2​α^+2n2​α^+1​,rx​y=cx​y2​.\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)=\frac{2\hat{\alpha}+\frac{2}{n}}{2\hat{\alpha}+1}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad r_{xy}=\frac{c_{xy}}{2}\;\text{.}

On the complete graph G=KnG=K_{n} with cx​y≡1nc_{xy}\equiv\frac{1}{n}, it is immediate to check that gap1​(G,α)=12{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)=\frac{1}{2}. Hence, Theorem 2.11 yields the following lower bound for gap⁡(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha):

(5.12) γKMP​(G,α)​gap1​(G,α)=12​2​α^+2n2​α^+1​.\gamma_{\rm KMP}(G,\alpha)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)=\frac{1}{2}\frac{2\hat{\alpha}+\frac{2}{n}}{2\hat{\alpha}+1}\;\text{.}

According to [CLL20, Eq. (10)], this is precisely the spectral gap of the corresponding KMP{\rm KMP} model. Finally, recall that, in this homogeneous mean-field setting, the KMP model satisfies gap⁡(G,α)=gap2​(G,α){\rm gap}(G,\alpha)={\rm gap}_{2}(G,\alpha); see, e.g., [Cap08].

On the segment with homogeneous α≡α^≥1\alpha\equiv\hat{\alpha}\geq 1, [CLL20, Theorem 2] proves that the upper bound in Theorem 2.11 is, in fact, an identity. See [LP25, Theorem 3] for an analogous result on the segment with

(5.13) αx=α^​(1+σ1−σ)x−1​,x∈V={1,…,n}​,​α^≥1​,​σ∈(0,1)​.\alpha_{x}=\hat{\alpha}\left(\frac{1+\sigma}{1-\sigma}\right)^{x-1}\;\text{,}\;\;\qquad x\in V=\left\{1,\ldots,n\right\}\;\text{,}\;\;\hat{\alpha}\geq 1\;\text{,}\;\;\sigma\in(0,1)\;\text{.}

5.2. Harmonic process

Here, we have

(5.14) βx​y​(d​u,d​v)=cx​y​uαx−1​(1−u)−1​d​u⊗δ1​(d​v)​.\beta_{xy}({\rm d}u,{\rm d}v)=c_{xy}\,u^{\alpha_{x}-1}\left(1-u\right)^{-1}{\rm d}u\otimes\delta_{1}({\rm d}v)\;\text{.}

For reversibility, see, e.g., [FFG23, Appendix A] for the case α≡const.\alpha\equiv{\rm const.}; the general case is analogously verified.

With this choice, we obtain rx​y=cx​y​1αxr_{xy}=c_{xy}\,\frac{1}{\alpha_{x}}, for all x,y∈Vx,y\in V, and, clearly, these rates satisfy detailed balance with respect to π\pi given in (5.4). Further, we obtain

and, thus, the main conclusion of Theorem 1.2.

We now argue that the lower bound in Theorem 1.2 is attained on the homogeneous complete graph, that is, when cx​y≡1nc_{xy}\equiv\frac{1}{n} and α≡α^>0\alpha\equiv\hat{\alpha}>0. Indeed, in this case, we have gap1​(G,α)=α^−1{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)={\hat{\alpha}}^{-1} and

(5.18) γHP​(G,α)​gap1​(G,α)=2α^​α^+1nα^+1​.\gamma_{\rm HP}(G,\alpha)\,{\rm gap}_{1}(G,\alpha)=\frac{2}{\hat{\alpha}}\frac{\hat{\alpha}+\frac{1}{n}}{\hat{\alpha}+1}\;\text{.}

Here, fix κ∈(0,αmin)\kappa\in(0,\alpha_{\rm min}), and consider

(5.20) βx​y​(d​u,d​v)=cx​y2​B​(αx−κ,κ)​B​(αy−κ,κ)​uαx−κ−1​(1−u)κ−1​vαy−κ−1​(1−v)κ−1​d​u​d​v​.\beta_{xy}({\rm d}u,{\rm d}v)=\frac{c_{xy}}{2\,{\rm B}(\alpha_{x}-\kappa,\kappa)\,{\rm B}(\alpha_{y}-\kappa,\kappa)}\,u^{\alpha_{x}-\kappa-1}\left(1-u\right)^{\kappa-1}v^{\alpha_{y}-\kappa-1}\left(1-v\right)^{\kappa-1}\,{\rm d}u{\rm d}v\;\text{.}

Recall that we required κ<αmin\kappa<\alpha_{\rm min}; further, γIEM​(G,α,κ)≥1\gamma_{\rm IEM}(G,\alpha,\kappa)\geq 1 if αmin≥1+2​κ\alpha_{\rm min}\geq 1+2\kappa. Hence, under these conditions, the upper bound in Theorem 1.3 saturates to an identity. Corollary 2.14 leads to the same conclusion.

As similarly done in Section 5.2.1 for the HP, we show that on the homogeneous complete graph the lower bound is attained.
